# **Theoretical Foundations and Architectural Design of SynapseRT: An Edge-Cloud Context-Aware Knowledge Synthesis System**

## **Context-Aware Computing and Real-Time Session Classification**

The incorporation of interactive technologies into collaborative spaces has transitioned from static, user-commanded interfaces to fluid, proactive environments that adapt to human behavior in real time.1 Rather than treating user inputs as isolated commands, modern ubiquitous computing models aim to capture and decode the natural environment, allowing computers to transition into the background of human interaction.1 This design principle, first articulated by Mark Weiser in his seminal vision of ubiquitous computing, requires systems to capture, retrieve, and act upon environmental variables to support active human tasks.1  
The term "context-aware computing" was introduced by Bill Schilit and Marvin Theimer in 1994, who defined it as software that adapts dynamically based on its location of use, the collection of nearby people and objects, and changes to those entities over time.1 While early definitions relied on physical indicators, Anind Dey established a broader, more robust definition in 2001 that remains the standard for modern context-aware systems: context is any information that can be used to characterize the situation of an entity.1 An entity, in this framing, is a person, place, or object considered relevant to the interaction between a user and an application, including the user and the application themselves.1 Consequently, a system is context-aware if it uses context to provide relevant information or services to the user, with relevance directly tied to the user's active task.1  
Dey's framework outlines three core categories of features that a context-aware application can support:

* The presentation of information and services to a user.3  
* The automatic execution of a service for a user.3  
* The tagging of context to information to support later retrieval.3

SynapseRT operationalizes these three features by using real-time speech streams as its primary contextual input. Traditional context-aware platforms rely on physical sensor networks (such as active badges or infrared location sensors) to capture context.1 In contrast, SynapseRT treats the acoustic transcript of a meeting as a dynamic semantic environment. The system's session context classifier processes this stream to determine the active room mode (such as a pedagogical lecture, an open brainstorm, or a structured project review), thereby characterizing the collaborative situation.1

| Context Dimension | Traditional Ubiquitous Systems | SynapseRT System |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Primary Context Source** | Physical telemetry, GPS, infrared active badges, ambient sensors 1 | Live spoken language dialogue streams and transcription text |
| **Entity State Representation** | Spatial coordinates, device proximity, time-of-day logs 1 | Structural dialogue act transition matrices and semantic topic boundaries 4 |
| **Adaptation Mechanism** | Deterministic declarative rules and location-triggered software launches 1 | Dynamic language model prompting and adaptive interface rendering 6 |
| **Dey’s Feature 1: Presentation** | Displaying local maps or resource directories based on proximity 1 | Adjusting concept maps and sidebars to match user roles 6 |
| **Dey’s Feature 2: Execution** | Routing phone calls or adjusting climate controls based on room occupancy 1 | Modulating the routing threshold ![][image1] to prioritize either local processing or cloud escalation 9 |
| **Dey’s Feature 3: Tagging** | Appending location and timestamp metadata to captured files 3 | Structuring spoken dialogue acts and mapping them to visualization templates 5 |

By building upon this established taxonomy, the session context classifier shifts from a simple text-processing tool to a core context-aware component.1 It systematically translates the live conversation into an active contextual variable, enabling the system's visualization and agentic orchestration layers to adapt to the collaborative environment.1

## **Agentic Orchestration and Hybrid Edge-Cloud Tool Routing**

The core of SynapseRT's execution engine is an agentic orchestration harness designed to manage the trade-offs between processing latency, financial cost, and data privacy.10 This architecture is built upon the Reasoning and Acting (ReAct) paradigm developed by Yao et al. in 2022\.12 ReAct provides a framework that allows large language models (LLMs) to generate both deliberative thought traces and task-specific actions in an interleaved, sequential manner.13  
Historically, reasoning and acting in language models were studied as separate capabilities.14 Reasoning models focused on step-by-step internal deductions, while acting models focused on predicting action sequences in interactive environments.14 ReAct combines these two paradigms.13 The model generates a reasoning trace to create, track, and update action plans, and then executes an action to interact with external environments (such as APIs or databases) to gather new information.13 This thought-action-observation loop allows the model to handle exceptions dynamically, correct its plans based on real-world feedback, and ground its responses in external data, significantly reducing hallucination rates.11

               |             Real-Time Query (q)           |  
               \+---------------------+---------------------+  
                                     |  
                                     v  
                       \+-------------+-------------+  
                       |    Win Prediction Model   |  
                       |    P\_theta(wins | q)      |  
                       \+-------------+-------------+  
                                     |  
                                     | Calculate Win Probability  
                                     v  
                           /-------------------\\  
                          / P\_theta(wins | q)   \\  
                         \<      \>= alpha?        \>  
                          \\ (Cost Threshold)    /  
                           \\-------------------/  
                               /           \\  
                     No (Route Local)     Yes (Route Cloud)  
                             /               \\  
                            v                 v  
               \+------------+------------+  \+------------+------------+  
               |  Hermes 2 Pro (M\_weak)  |  | Frontier Model (M\_strong|  
               |  \- Local Edge GPU       |  | \- Hosted Cloud API      |  
               |  \- XML Function Calls   |  | \- High Cost / Latency   |  
               \+-------------------------+  \+-------------------------+

To deploy this agentic pattern at the local edge, SynapseRT uses open-weight models optimized for structured tool use, specifically Nous Research's Hermes 2 Pro.7 Hermes 2 Pro is fine-tuned on custom datasets designed for reliable tool use and structured JSON generation, scoring 90% on function calling evaluations conducted with Fireworks.AI and 84% on structured JSON output validation.7 The model uses a ChatML prompt structure that establishes clear roles for multi-turn dialogue.7 During operation, it parses system-defined XML schemas to execute local tools, managing the ReAct loop without requiring constant cloud connectivity.16  
To balance local processing with cloud capabilities, SynapseRT implements a selective hybrid routing framework based on RouteLLM.10 This framework optimizes resource allocation by routing simpler, privacy-sensitive requests to the local model (![][image2]), while escalating complex conceptual requests to a cloud-hosted frontier model (![][image3]).10  
The routing decision is modeled as a binary classification problem.9 Let ![][image4] represent the user prompt or the transcribed dialogue segment. A win-prediction model calculates the probability ![][image5] that the strong model will outperform the weak model for that specific query.9 This prediction model is trained on comparative human preference data from platforms like Chatbot Arena.9 The training objective maximizes the log-likelihood of the preference outcomes 10:  
![][image6]  
where ![][image7] represents the pairwise comparison label indicating whether the strong model won, tied with, or lost to the weak model on query ![][image4].10  
The actual routing decision ![][image8] is governed by a tunable cost-quality threshold $\\alpha \\in $ 9:  
![][image9]  
![][image10]  
The cost-quality threshold ![][image1] serves as a controller for the system 9:

* **High ![][image1] (Cost & Privacy Focus):** Forces queries to be handled by the local model, minimizing API costs and keeping sensitive data on local hardware.9  
* **Low ![][image1] (Quality & Capability Focus):** Allows queries to be escalated to cloud models, providing high response quality for complex synthesis tasks.9

| Orchestration Paradigm | Operational Execution Model | Latency Profile | Primary Failure Modes | SynapseRT Application |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Chain-of-Thought (CoT)** | Generates step-by-step reasoning traces internally prior to producing final output. | Moderate (proportional to reasoning token count). | Factual hallucinations and error propagation in long sequences.11 | Offline narrative synthesis and summarization. |
| **ReAct Framework** | Interleaves reasoning traces with tool execution, using external feedback.13 | High (due to sequential API calls and environmental delays).11 | Latency overhead, tool execution errors, and dependency on source quality.11 | Real-time tool execution on the Hermes 2 Pro edge node.16 |
| **Cascading & Verification** | Queries models sequentially, verifying outputs before potentially escalating.10 | High cumulative latency (multiple generation cycles).10 | Accumulation of verification errors and high inference latency.10 | Offline post-session validation of summary records. |
| **RouteLLM Hybrid Routing** | Uses a win-prediction model to route queries to a single model *before* generation.10 | Low (routing decision introduces minimal computational overhead).10 | Misclassification of query complexity, leading to suboptimal routing.10 | Real-time context routing between edge and cloud systems.9 |

Rather than keeping the threshold ![][image1] static, SynapseRT connects it directly to the session context classifier. When the room mode is classified as highly confidential or low-complexity, the classifier increases the threshold (![][image11]), enforcing local processing.10 When the session is classified as a complex, collaborative research meeting, the system lowers the threshold (![][image12]), allowing the agentic harness to escalate complex tasks to cloud frontier models to ensure high-quality synthesis.9

## **Information Salience, Dialogue Segmentation, and Relevance Filtering**

Isolating key decisions and action items from real-time multi-party discussions requires filtering out casual, non-essential dialogue.19 To achieve this, SynapseRT models information salience using the annotations and dialogue act (DA) classifications established in the AMI Meeting Corpus.5 The AMI corpus consists of 100 hours of multi-party meeting recordings annotated for transcription, topic segmentation, summaries, and speaker intentions.4  
Multi-party conversations are often informal and filled with overlapping speech, meaning they lack clear sentence boundaries.19 To handle this, SynapseRT segments the raw transcript stream into discrete dialogue act units based on acoustic pauses and speaker transitions.19 The AMI classification scheme organizes these dialogue acts into 15 distinct types across five major categories, helping the system identify speaker intentions (such as exchanging information or initiating group action).5

| Major DA Grouping | Core Dialogue Act Types (AMI Schema) | SynapseRT Processing Pipeline | Visual Taxonomy Destination |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Information Exchange** | Statement, Strong Statement, Inform, Description 5 | Evaluated for conceptual density and noun-phrase relationships. | Force-Directed Knowledge Graph 8 |
| **Action & Commitment** | Suggestion, Offer, Action-Item Commitment 5 | Routed to extractive summarization and temporal parsing.20 | Kanban Boards & Timelines 8 |
| **Social / Backchannel** | Chit-Chat, Positive Assessment, Backchannel Noise 5 | Identified as low-salience content and filtered out of active processing.19 | Background Archive Log Only |
| **Topic Transitions** | Topic Shift, Agenda Setting, Session Boundary 4 | Triggers topic segmentation and mind-map updates.4 | Hierarchical Mind Map 8 |
| **Clarification Loop** | Question, Request Info, Elicit Comment 5 | Monitored for unresolved questions to track session engagement.6 | Facilitator Analytics Panel 6 |

To train and evaluate the salience engine, SynapseRT adopts the gold-standard labeling process from the AMI Meeting Corpus.19 In the AMI corpus, human annotators wrote abstractive summaries and linked individual summary sentences directly to the underlying transcript dialogue acts that supported them.19 This linking structure allows the system to calculate an objective Gold Standard Value (![][image13]) for each segment.19  
Let ![][image14] represent the number of independent annotators assigned to a session, and let ![][image15] indicate whether annotator ![][image16] linked dialogue act segment ![][image17] to a summary sentence.19 If annotators distinguish between essential and optional sentences, essential links are weighted three times higher than optional ones (![][image18] for essential, ![][image19] for optional).24 The ![][image13] for a segment ![][image17] is calculated as 19:  
![][image20]  
For binary salience classification, dialogue acts are ranked by their ![][image13], and the top-ranked segments (e.g., the top 30% of word count) are extracted as positive, salient instances, while the remainder are classified as negative background chatter.19  
The performance of the salience classifier is evaluated using weighted precision and weighted recall metrics, which account for multi-annotator linking variations.19 High-agreement datasets are challenging to build because what constitutes a salient point can be subjective.19 This subjectivity is reflected in the low inter-rater agreement on the AMI corpus, which reports a Cohen's kappa value of 0.48.19 To improve performance, SynapseRT compares its outputs against alternative corpora, such as the Kyutech Corpus, which uses explicit importance tags linked to consensus summaries.22 This multi-corpus approach helps train a salience classifier that can reliably isolate key information from real-time dialogue.19

## **Visual Form Taxonomy and Cognitive Sensemaking**

Presenting real-time meeting structures to users in a shared workspace requires a visual design that reduces cognitive load. To prevent its interface from appearing arbitrary, SynapseRT bases its visual mappings on Ben Shneiderman’s classic "Task by Data Type Taxonomy for Information Visualizations".8 Shneiderman's taxonomy maps seven distinct data types to specific visual structures and outlines a standard interaction pattern: overview first, zoom and filter, then details-on-demand.8  
By analyzing the data structure of incoming dialogue acts, SynapseRT automatically maps extracted information to Shneiderman's taxonomic categories, transforming raw transcripts into structured visual interfaces.5

  Live Speech Stream \-\> Dialogue Act Segmentation \-\> Data Structure Mapping \-\> Shneiderman Visual Form  
    
  \---\> \[ Action-Oriented \] \----\> \------\>  
    
  \----------\> \---------\> \[ Network \] \-------\>  
    
  \-------\> \[ Hierarchical \] \--------\> \----------\> \[ Nested Mind Map \]  
    
  \-----------\> \----\> \--------\>

* **Action-Oriented Acts and Temporal Data:** Spoken dialogue segments classified under the AMI schema as action commitments, suggestions, or deadlines map directly to Shneiderman's *Temporal* data type.5 These are rendered as dynamic, sequential timelines and Kanban boards, transforming verbal commitments into structured project tasks.20  
* **Entity Associations and Network Data:** Spoken segments containing relational nouns, concept dependencies, or technological terms map to the *Network* data type.8 These are visualized as real-time, force-directed knowledge graphs, illustrating how ideas and dependencies connect across a session.  
* **Topic Hierarchies and Tree Data:** Spoken shifts in conversation, parsed via topic-segmentation models, map to the *Tree* data type.4 These are displayed as nested hierarchical mind maps, allowing users to view the parent-child relationships of different discussion topics.20  
* **Conceptual Definitions and One-Dimensional Data:** Simple noun-phrase definitions and terminology clarifications map to *One-Dimensional* textual lists.8 These are hidden by default and displayed in sidebar panels only when a user selects a node, adhering to Shneiderman’s details-on-demand design principle.8

| Target Data Type (Shneiderman Taxonomy) | Spoken Semantic Structure | Interactive UI Modality | Collaborative Sensemaking Function |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Temporal Data** 8 | Action commitments, deadlines, and project milestones.5 | Dynamic, sequential Kanban timeline. | Tracks task ownership and schedules deliverables.20 |
| **Network Data** 8 | Relational nouns and conceptual dependencies.8 | Force-directed link graph. | Maps complex conceptual connections and dependencies. |
| **Tree Data** 8 | Topic segments and conversation shifts.4 | Nested hierarchical mind map. | Visualizes the overall structure and flow of the discussion.4 |
| **One-Dimensional Data** 8 | Concept definitions and speaker profiles.8 | Detail-on-demand sidebar panel.8 | Provides contextual information without cluttering the main interface.8 |

This structured visual mapping supports collaborative sensemaking by mirroring human cognitive models. Converting spoken paths into persistent graphical networks reduces the cognitive effort required to track complex discussions, turning ephemeral conversations into stable, interactive knowledge structures.

## **Role-Aware Rendering and Collaborative Orchestration**

Collaborative workspaces involve participants with different informational needs. Rather than forcing all users to view the same interface, SynapseRT uses role-based visual filters to tailor the display of information to each user's specific functional responsibilities.  
This role-based design is modeled on Pierre Dillenbourg's "Orchestration Graphs," which formalize synchronous workflows in collaborative learning environments.6 Orchestration Graphs define the progression of collaborative tasks and outline how information is captured, transformed, and shared among different roles.6

                     \+----------------------------------+  
                     |  Shared Semantic Knowledge Base  |  
                     |  (Unified Conceptual Graph)      |  
                     \+----------------+-----------------+  
                                      |  
         \+----------------------------+----------------------------+  
         |                            |                            |  
         v                            v                            v  
\+--------+--------+          \+--------+--------+          \+--------+--------+  
| Facilitator View |          |  Student View   |          | Note-Taker View |  
|                 |          |                 |          |                 |  
| \- Aggregate     |          | \- Highlighted   |          | \- Draft Summary |  
|   Analytics     |          |   Concept Maps  |          |   Edits         |  
| \- Participation |          | \- Definition    |          | \- Action Item   |  
|   Telemetry     |          |   Sidebars      |          |   Validation    |  
\+-----------------+          \+-----------------+          \+-----------------+

By decoupling the underlying conceptual graph from the user interface, SynapseRT processes a single, unified session state while rendering custom dashboards for different roles:

* **The Facilitator / Instructor:** This role requires macro-level analytical visualizations.6 The system renders high-level participation telemetry, consensus tracking, and real-time cognitive load indicators based on dialogue act distributions.5 This allows the facilitator to monitor overall session progress and balance discussion contributions.  
* **The Active Learner / Participant:** This role requires conceptual scaffolding. The system displays micro-level conceptual visual aids, including hierarchical topic maps, node-link diagrams of technical relationships, and real-time definitions in on-demand sidebars.6  
* **The Note-Taker / Recorder:** This role requires editorial control over the group's record. The system provides a chronological dashboard displaying draft Action Items, decision points, and summarized bullet points, allowing the note-taker to quickly edit and approve key takeaways.20

| Target Audience Role | Primary Information Needs | Visual Modality Design | Dillenbourg Orchestration Task |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Facilitator / Instructor** | Tracking group dynamics, conceptual coverage, and participation balances.6 | Macro aggregate analytics dashboard and participation timelines. | Monitors group progress, identifies discussion gaps, and manages pacing.6 |
| **Participant / Student** | Understanding key concepts, terminology definitions, and structural relationships.8 | Force-directed graphs and nested mind maps with details-on-demand.8 | Supports individual comprehension and structural learning.6 |
| **Note-Taker / Recorder** | Verifying decisions, tracking action items, and drafting summary text.20 | Chronological edit interface with draft action cards and validation tools.20 | Validates and exports the official record of the session.20 |

By implementing these adaptive visual modes, SynapseRT resolves the tension between individual learning needs and group synchronization.6 Each role interacts with a tailored visual interface, while the underlying system maintains a unified, synchronized representation of the session's context.3

## **Architectural Performance and Execution Profile**

To demonstrate the viability of deploying SynapseRT in real-time collaborative environments, the system's runtime parameters are dynamically configured based on the classified session mode. This approach ensures that resource-intensive cloud processing is reserved for complex discussions, while simpler sessions are handled by efficient local models.10

| Architectural Parameter | Local Edge Mode (Nous Hermes 2 Pro) | Cloud-Escalated Mode (Frontier Model) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Hardware Deployment** | Local edge GPU node (offline/on-premise deployment) 16 | Publicly hosted API cloud clusters 10 |
| **Parameter Scale** | **![][image21]** to ![][image22] parameters 7 | Proprietary mixture-of-experts scale |
| **Syntax Formatting** | ChatML with XML-tagged tool signatures 7 | Cloud-native structured JSON formatting |
| **Function Calling Baseline** | 90% (Fireworks.AI Evaluation) 7 | Near-perfect API validation baseline |
| **Structured JSON Baseline** | 84% (Nous Research Evaluation) 7 | High-accuracy schema enforcement |
| **Routing Metric Constraint** | Assigned when $P\_\\theta(\\text{wins} | q) \< \\alpha$ 9 |
| **Operational Costs** | Low marginal runtime cost (local computation) | High API call-volume costs 10 |
| **Data Privacy Level** | Zero external data transmission (strict local storage) | Subject to external API data policies 11 |

By maintaining a unified database of session contexts, SynapseRT coordinates ReAct-based tool orchestration, salience filtering, and role-adaptive rendering in a continuous execution loop.3 The session classifier continually assesses the conversational context to dynamically adjust the routing threshold ![][image1], balancing processing latency, security, and conceptual depth based on the group's active needs.3

## **Evaluative Framework and Capstone Defense Strategy**

To defend the academic viability of SynapseRT before a capstone evaluation panel, the system's performance must be measured against established benchmarks in natural language processing and human-computer interaction. The evaluation strategy uses a two-pronged approach, focusing on technical model accuracy and human-centric usability.

                         \+-----------------------------+  
                         |  SynapseRT Evaluation Plans |  
                         \+--------------+--------------+  
                                        |  
         \+------------------------------+------------------------------+  
         |                                                             |  
         v                                                             v  
\+--------+----------------------+                            \+---------+--------------------+  
| Technical Model Accuracy      |                            | Human-Centric Usability      |  
|                               |                            |                              |  
| \- Dialogue Act Parsing        |                            | \- Collaborative Sensemaking  |  
| \- Extractive Summarization    |                            | \- Orchestration Efficiency   |  
| \- System Latency Profiles     |                            | \- User Trust Assessment      |  
\+-------------------------------+                            \+------------------------------+

### **Technical Accuracy Benchmarks**

* **Dialogue Act Classification:** The performance of the live segmentation and parsing models is measured against the AMI Meeting Corpus test set.4 The target baseline is to match or exceed the standard F1-score for 15-class dialogue act classification on multi-party speech.23  
* **Extractive Summarization Accuracy:** The salience engine's performance is validated using the gold-standard annotator links of the AMI scenario meetings.19 System-generated summaries are evaluated using weighted precision and weighted recall metrics, with a target performance goal of outperforming traditional non-adaptive extractive baselines.19  
* **Orchestration Harness Latency:** The system evaluates routing efficiency by measuring response times across different threshold values (![][image1]).9 This profile tracks the latency savings achieved by routing simpler queries to local edge nodes rather than escalating all requests to cloud hosts.10

### **Usability and Collaboration Metrics**

* **Collaborative Sensemaking Support:** Controlled user studies compare groups using SynapseRT's dynamic visual interfaces with control groups using raw text transcripts.6 Cognitive load is measured using the NASA-TLX index to assess whether Shneiderman-mapped visual representations successfully reduce mental fatigue during complex discussions.8  
* **Orchestration Efficiency:** Evaluators assess how well the role-based dashboards support group synchronization.6 This study measures the time note-takers spend editing summary records and the accuracy with which facilitators identify participation imbalances.6  
* **User Trust Assessment:** The evaluation tracks user trust regarding data handling.11 By prompting users after sessions, studies evaluate whether the system's dynamic edge-routing model successfully addresses privacy concerns during highly confidential discussions.10

This dual evaluation strategy provides a rigorous foundation for SynapseRT, showing how its technical components align with established research in context-aware computing, agentic orchestration, and information visualization. By framing every design choice around recognized academic literature, the capstone presentation demonstrates a systematic approach to building collaborative knowledge synthesis systems.
